increments.title: The authoring rules pick a rule's form by the failure it prevents
increments.goal: Whoever edits a page in this repository finds in the authoring rules a four-row table that picks the form of a correction from the failure class it prevents, and a standing ban on patching a working rule with an exemption clause. Today that choice is made by taste and re-learned through failed agent runs.
criteria: The authoring rules carry a table of exactly four rows; each row names a failure class, the form that works against it, the form that fails against it, and the reason in one sentence.

The four rows are: a rule skipped under pressure gets a prohibition carrying its price and the verbatim rationalisation it counters; a wrong output shape gets a recipe stating what the output is; an omitted required element gets a required slot in the schema or template; behaviour that depends on a condition gets a rule keyed to an observable predicate.
The authoring rules forbid patching an existing rule with an exemption clause and require re-cutting the rule on an observable predicate instead.

The table and the exemption rule reach whoever authors a skill page and whoever authors an agent page alike, and the repository's existing rule about one home per rule is not broken to achieve it — no page restates what another page already carries.
The commands the increment names all exit 0.

SCOPE. Increment 1 is the four-row form table and the ban on exemption clauses, reaching whoever authors a skill page and whoever authors an agent page alike. DECISION 1 — THE HOME. Create a new page `.claude/rules/authoring.md`, path-scoped to both audiences:

---
paths:
  - "skills/**"
  - "agents/**"
---

Why there. The rule binds whoever *writes* a page in this checkout, not an agent at run time. `.claude/rules/agents.md` (lines 58-63) states the test: a page under `.claude/rules/` may only carry what someone developing uroboros needs, and may never be the only home of a rule that binds a run. An authoring rule for uroboros's own prose pages is exactly the first and not the second. The same page (lines 15-20) records the measured mechanic this relies on: a path-scoped rule is not inherited at launch, but a reader that opens a matching file loads it for itself, subagents included. So one page reaches both authoring audiences with no restatement anywhere and no hop. Confirmed against the Claude Code memory docs ('Path-specific rules'): `paths` takes a YAML list of glob patterns, and path-scoped rules trigger when a matching file is read. Confirmed against `test-repo.sh` lines 99-105: its `scope.js` parser already reads the list form, so the two existing cases in the '=== no repository-local rule reaches an agent' section (every rules page is scoped; every pattern matches tracked files) guard the new page for free, with no change to them.

Rejected alternatives.
(a) `skills/agent-brief/SKILL.md`, the shared brief. `skills/CLAUDE.md`'s 'Where a rule belongs' sends a rule that binds more than one skill or agent to the brief, but that section is about rules that bind agents *at run time* — its own justification is 'Nothing else reaches every agent'. The brief ships with the plugin and is injected into every agent on every run in every project; the planner, reviewer, test-author and researcher never author a uroboros page, and no installing project has uroboros pages to author. `.claude/rules/agents.md` lines 46-47 draw the same line: 'This page is for whoever writes the agents; the shared brief is for the agents.'
(b) The table in `skills/CLAUDE.md`, with a pointer from `.claude/rules/agents.md`. Rejected: that page is titled 'The skills' and loads only for a reader working under `skills/`, so an agent-page author reaches the rule only through a hop that costs a read and can be skipped. Criterion 4 asks that it reach both alike.
(c) One rules page scoped `**/*.md`. Rejected: it matches `docs/issues/**`, so every agent that reads its issue file would load the authoring rules it has no use for.

DECISION 2 — WHAT THE NEW PAGE SAYS. Keep it short (roughly 30-40 lines) and in this order:

1. Title `# The form of a rule`.
2. One framing sentence: the rows below come from measured head-to-head wording tests (obra/superpowers, `skills/writing-skills/SKILL.md`, 'Match the Form to the Failure'), so a row changes on a measurement and not on taste.
3. One markdown table — the only table on the page — with the header `Failure class | Form that works | Form that fails | Why` and exactly four body rows:

   - A wrong output shape | A recipe that states what the output is | A list of prohibitions | A ban names what not to emit and leaves the shape unstated, which measured worse than no guidance at all.
   - An omitted required element | A required slot in the schema or the template | Prose in the body asking for the element | A slot makes the omission visible in the artefact, while prose is satisfied by an agent that believes it complied.
   - Behaviour that depends on a condition | A rule keyed to an observable predicate | A judgement call, or an exemption bolted onto the general rule | A predicate the agent can evaluate decides both branches, and a judgement call decides neither.
4. The ban, as its own short paragraph below the table, in the imperative: never patch a working rule with an exemption clause; re-cut the rule on an observable predicate instead, stating the two branches separately — one appended exemption measured a working rule down from consistent to noisy.
5. One closing sentence saying why the page is repo-local: it binds whoever writes a page here rather than an agent at run time, so it stays out of the shipped brief.

- The ban paragraph also carries 're-cut' and 'observable predicate'.
- The word 'rationalisation' likewise appears on this page alone outside `docs/issues/`.
